To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mineral phase of caries-attacted enamel has lower crystallinity, contains non-apatitic phases and has a lower degree of microcrystallite alignment.
the apatite crystallite size and the degree of alignment are reduced in caries-attacted enamel, and the apatite is partially replaced with non-apatitic phases.
enamel apatitic crystals in white spot lesions have lower crystallinity than those in sound enamel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mineral phase of the caries-affected enamel and its relationship to the demineralization and remineralization process.
the crystallographic alterations of enamel apatite and the occurrence of non- apatitic minerals in the early stage of enamel caries.
the crystallographic, structural, and chemical alterations in the mineral phases of human enamel with the onset and progress of caries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mineral phase of the enamel with carious attack has a different crystalline structure and a different microcrystallinity from that of undamaged enamel.
enamel apatites in white spot lesions are less crystalline, less aligned and more porous than the apatites in sound enamel.
the demineralization and remineralization processes are responsible for the observed alterations in the mineral phases and crystallographic properties of the enamel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mineral phase in the white spot lesions is not only demineralized but also altered in crystallographic and/or structural properties.

the caries process involves a complex series of events, including the formation of a non-apatitic phase, followed by the remineralization process, which is accompanied by a change in the microcrystallinity of the apatite phase and a change in the orientation of the apatites.
the mineral phase of caries-attacking enamel undergoes structural and crystallographic changes which can be explained in terms of the remineralization process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the crystalline structure of the apatitic phase of the mineral phase of caries-attacking enamel is different from that of the apatite mineral phase of sound enamel.
the mineral phase of carious enamel undergoes structural changes that may affect the properties of enamel.
X-ray diffraction and ESR are useful tools for investigating the structural changes in the enamel with the onset and progression of caries.
